In ==type 1 diabetes== (T1D), meals, subcutaneous insulin, and physical activity are not independent inputs. Each initiates a time-varying process, and the observed glucose trajectory reflects their overlap with the current physiological state.

[Back to module index](index.qmd) · [Glucose–insulin system](glucose-insulin-system.qmd)

## Meals: appearance is a process, not an instant event

Ingested carbohydrate must be dispersed, digested to monosaccharides, transported through intestinal cells, and pass through the portal circulation before it contributes to systemic glucose. Gastric emptying is an important determinant of glucose appearance; its contribution depends on meal composition, gastric function, and population ([Horowitz et al., 1993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8405758/); [Marathe et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23613599/)).

Meal form and composition alter that time course:

- Liquids bypass much of the mechanical processing required for solids and usually empty faster.
- Intact food structure and viscous fibre delay the availability and diffusion of digestible carbohydrate ([Würsch and Pi-Sunyer, 1997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9353622/)).
- Fat activates intestinal feedback that slows gastric emptying and can shift part of the glucose response later ([Marathe et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23613599/)).
- Protein contributes amino acids, stimulates glucagon, and can support delayed gluconeogenesis; its net glycaemic effect depends on carbohydrate, fat, insulin, and context ([Paterson et al., 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26499756/); [Bell et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25998293/)).

The ==glycaemic index== (GI) summarises the post-meal glucose response to a fixed amount of available carbohydrate, but it combines several mechanisms into one empirical ranking. Food preparation, matrix, fibre, fat, gastric emptying, and individual response all limit its precision ([Jenkins et al., 1981](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6259925/); [Bell et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25998293/)).

::: {.callout-important title="Evidence and design inference"}
Carbohydrate amount alone does not determine the post-meal trajectory ([Bell et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25998293/)). **Design inference:** a game that gives every meal the same absorption curve will erase an important learning objective: rapid, delayed, and prolonged glucose appearance can occur with the same nominal carbohydrate content.
:::

## Subcutaneous insulin: depot, circulation, action

Pharmaceutical insulin must first leave the subcutaneous depot. Formulation chemistry, dose volume, local blood flow, temperature, accidental intramuscular delivery, anatomical site, and tissue condition influence absorption. Absorption from the depot can prolong the apparent time course substantially beyond clearance of circulating insulin; a single plasma half-life should not be used as the duration of subcutaneous insulin action ([Gradel et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30116732/), sections on the absorption process and physiological factors).

Rapid-acting analogues destabilise insulin self-association to accelerate absorption. Basal analogues use precipitation, albumin binding, or multi-hexamer formation to prolong release. These strategies alter average profiles but do not eliminate within-person or between-person variability ([Heinemann, 2002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12450450/); [Haahr and Heise, 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25179915/)).

The effect profile is also not equivalent to the concentration profile. Receptor signalling, glucose transporter recruitment, suppression of hepatic glucose output, and tissue-specific sensitivity add delay and shape. “Insulin on board” is therefore an operational approximation of residual activity, not a directly observed physiological quantity.

## Exercise: different modes, different balances

Muscle contraction recruits ==glucose transporter type 4== (GLUT4) through signalling that is partly independent of insulin. Contraction and insulin can therefore have additive effects on muscle glucose uptake ([Sylow et al., 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27739515/)).

During continuous moderate aerobic activity, muscle uptake commonly rises faster than hepatic glucose production when circulating insulin is active, favouring a glucose fall. The risk can persist after activity because glycogen restoration and increased insulin sensitivity continue. Experimental evidence, including studies in people without diabetes and the human/animal literature reviewed by Cartee, supports enhanced insulin-stimulated uptake during recovery. It does not establish a universal 48-hour response in T1D; magnitude and duration depend on activity, fitness, glycogen status, and population ([Mikines et al., 1988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3126668/); [Cartee, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4816200/)).

High-intensity intervals and resistance exercise evoke stronger catecholamine responses and hepatic glucose release. Their immediate glucose direction is more context-dependent than steady aerobic activity. In a meta-analysis of high-intensity interval exercise in adults with T1D, fasted sessions tended to raise glucose while postprandial sessions tended to lower it, illustrating the importance of active insulin and meal state ([McClure et al., 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36549943/)). Resistance exercise is often less glucose-lowering during the bout than aerobic exercise, but can still be followed by later glucose lowering ([Yardley et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23172972/)).

## Interaction matrix

**Mechanistic synthesis and design inference**, based on the sources discussed above; these qualitative patterns are not individual predictions.

| Process | Primary near-term effect | Important delayed effect | Main source of uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rapidly absorbed carbohydrate | Raises glucose appearance | Usually limited tail | Gastric emptying, food form, starting state |
| Mixed high-fat meal | May delay early appearance | Can prolong the post-meal rise | Composition, meal size, gastric motility |
| Rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin | Increases peripheral disposal and suppresses hepatic output after an absorption delay | Residual action can outlast early meal appearance | Depot absorption, site, temperature, dose volume |
| Moderate aerobic activity | Increases contraction-mediated uptake | Increased insulin sensitivity and glycogen restoration | Active insulin, intensity, duration, glycogen state |
| Intense or resistance activity | Raises uptake and may strongly raise hepatic output | Later insulin sensitisation | Prandial state, catecholamines, fitness, protocol |

### Evidence limitations

- Controlled exercise studies are often small and use specific fitness levels, insulin conditions, meal states, and activity protocols.
- Meal studies vary in food form, macronutrient composition, gastric-motility status, and outcome definition.
- Average pharmacokinetic curves conceal substantial within-person variability.
- Evidence on fat and protein supports delayed effects, but no single universal conversion rule is valid across meals and individuals.

## Implications for serious-game design

::: {.callout-note title="Modelling and design inference"}
1. Use time-distributed events rather than instant changes.
2. Allow the player to inspect overlapping meal appearance, insulin action, and activity effects as separate conceptual layers.
3. Give meals a small number of physiologically interpretable profiles—such as rapid, mixed, and delayed—rather than claiming food-specific precision.
4. Separate continuous aerobic activity from high-intensity and resistance activity; their acute glucose directions are not interchangeable.
5. Carry exercise effects into recovery. Ending all effects when the activity animation stops teaches the wrong time scale.
6. Do not turn simulated responses into personal carbohydrate or insulin recommendations.
:::
